description:
I'm a high school student from India with experience in machine learning, research, and software development. For this challenge, I'm building IGNIS, a platform that uses NASA's microgravity combustion data to analyze experiments, model fire behavior, and help identify what scientists should test next.

I'm currently working solo and looking for people interested in physics, scientific computing, ML, or UI/UX. I want us to build something genuinely impressive, not just another AI dashboard.
summary:
IGNIS is an interactive website I built to make NASA's microgravity fire research easier to explore and understand. 

It brings together 66 source-linked evidence passages from six NASA investigations covering combustion, smoke and fire safety. 

Users can search the findings, compare experiments, check whether a safety claim is supported by the available evidence, and explore a published combustion equation. 

The search combines keyword retrieval with a pretrained language-embedding model that runs in the browser. Results link back to NASA's original research. 

IGNIS helps people understand what the experiments found, how their conditions differ, and when the evidence is not enough to give a reliable answer.
details:
I started IGNIS while looking into how fire behaves in microgravity. NASA has conducted experiments involving burning solid materials, smoke particles and liquid fuels, but the findings are spread across different investigations and technical reports. I wanted to make it easier to find the relevant research and understand what each experiment actually tells us.

IGNIS is a website built around 66 source-linked evidence passages from six NASA investigations: BASS-II, Saffire-I, SAME, SAME-R, FLEX and CFI-G. I kept these investigations separate because they used different materials, conditions and measurement methods. A finding about smoke particles, for example, cannot automatically support a claim about solid-fuel flammability.

The main feature, Mission Intelligence, uses BM25 keyword search and a pretrained MiniLM embedding model to retrieve relevant passages. The embedding model runs locally in the browser through ONNX. It helps rank information but does not write the scientific answers. Results are drawn from the evidence collection and link to original NASA sources.

I evaluated the retrieval methods on 14 source-linked questions using Recall@5. This is a small test, not a general performance claim. I used it to compare keyword and combined keyword-and-semantic search rather than assuming the embedding model improved results.

Research Atlas lets users explore relationships between investigations and inspect their experimental conditions and findings.

Evidence Stress Test examines whether a proposed conclusion is supported by the available research. For example, if someone asks whether PMMA is safe at 30% oxygen under lunar gravity, IGNIS can find related BASS-II findings. Those experiments do not establish a safety verdict under those exact conditions. The tool explains that limitation instead of inventing an answer.

Combustion Lab provides an interactive visualization of a published NASA equation for PMMA rods in opposed airflow. Users can change the strain rate and observe the oxygen boundary calculated from the equation.

Gravity Lab uses a simplified Boussinesq model to compute temperature and flow fields in a heated cavity at selectable gravity levels. It models nonreacting thermal transport, not a fire or spacecraft-material safety.

The site is built with React and TypeScript. I used Codex and Antigravity for coding assistance, debugging and software review, and ChatGPT to help edit explanations. The browser search uses a pretrained MiniLM embedding model.
